opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I learned from working with Kaiming is that a strong baseline isn't a boring preliminary step before the "real" research. In many ways, it *is* the research.

When people look at papers like ResNet, or later work like Mask R-CNN, MoCo, and MAE, they often see a clever new idea. What's less visible is how much effort goes into making the simplest version of something work really well. Kaiming has an almost obsessive discipline about this. Before you add anything, you have to understand very honestly where you stand. What does the plain version actually achieve if you tune it properly, train it long enough, and remove all the unnecessary tricks? Very often the answer surprises you. The simple thing is much stronger than the field assumes. Or it fails in a very specific, informative way, and that failure tells you what actually matters.

That shaped how I think about breakthroughs. I used to think breakthroughs come from complexity, some elaborate new module or a big theoretical insight. Now I think they more often come from clarity. If your baseline is weak, almost any idea looks like it helps, and you end up with a lot of noise in the literature: methods that seem to work but really just compensate for a poorly set-up starting point. If your baseline is strong, most ideas stop working, and the few that survive are real. Those are the ones that last.

There's also a taste component. Kaiming's work has a kind of minimalism: if you can remove a component and nothing gets worse, remove it. ResNeXt, which I worked on with him, was very much in that spirit. We weren't trying to invent a complicated architecture. We were trying to find a simple, repeatable design principle, and the strategy of using the same transformation many times turned out to be a cleaner way to scale than hand-designing every block. That way of thinking, asking "what is the simplest thing that captures the essence," has stayed with me in everything since.

The last thing I'd say is that strong baselines are a form of honesty, both with yourself and with the community. Research incentives push you to show that your method wins. A strong baseline forces you to ask whether you've actually learned something about the world, or whether you've just found a way to make a table look good. I think the people who consistently produce breakthroughs are the ones who are willing to be brutally honest at that stage. Kaiming is probably the best example of that I've seen.

r001.rationale: The response says strong baselines help distinguish real ideas, but does not state that baseline quality sets an upper limit on the research built on it.

r002.rationale: It explains that a weak baseline can make almost any idea appear helpful, when it may only compensate for a poorly set-up starting point.

r003.rationale: It presents a strong, properly tuned baseline as a test: ideas that still work against it are real and reflect learning, rather than merely making a results table look good.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing I learned from Kaiming, more than any specific technique, is that a strong baseline is not a chore you do before the real work. It is the real work.

When I first started working with him at FAIR, my instinct, like most grad students, was to go straight for the clever idea. You have a hypothesis, you build something complicated around it, and you compare against whatever number is in the previous paper. Kaiming would look at that and say, essentially, you haven't earned the right to make that comparison yet. First make the simple thing as good as it can possibly be. Train it longer. Fix the learning rate schedule. Check the data augmentation. Make sure the evaluation is actually fair. Very often, after you do that, the baseline has already caught up to the fancy method, and the question you were going to ask has dissolved.

That sounds humble, almost boring, but it has a huge effect on what you can discover. If your baseline is weak, every signal you see is contaminated. You can't tell whether your idea works or whether you just accidentally fixed a bug. A strong baseline cleans the signal. So when something does move the number, you can actually trust it, and you can trust it enough to push on it hard.

ResNet is the obvious example. The core idea is almost embarrassingly simple, an identity shortcut. What made it a breakthrough wasn't that nobody had thought of skip connections. It was that the whole thing was built on such a carefully controlled foundation that when depth went from twenty layers to a hundred and the result got better, there was no ambiguity about why. The simplicity was the point. He is very allergic to tricks that only work in one setting.

For me, ConvNeXt was really a direct application of that philosophy. The field had mostly decided transformers had won in vision, and the convnet was being treated as a 2015 artifact. We asked, what if we just give the ConvNet the same modern training recipe, the same design decisions, one at a time, and see what happens? No new operator, nothing exotic. And it turned out the gap was mostly a baseline gap, not an architecture gap. That paper only exists because of the way Kaiming taught me to think.

The broader lesson I've taken, and I try to pass it to my own students at NYU, is that breakthroughs in this field usually aren't a single flash of insight. They come from being obsessively honest about what is actually working, removing everything that isn't necessary, and then being bold once you have that solid ground. Kaiming has this rare combination of being extremely conservative about methodology and extremely ambitious about the question. Most people have one or the other. I think the combination is what enables real progress.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong baseline creates solid ground for research, but it does not state that baseline quality sets an upper limit on later research.

r002.rationale: It says a weak baseline contaminates the signal, making it hard to tell whether an idea worked or a bug was fixed.

r003.rationale: It explains that after making the baseline as strong as possible, a result that improves the number can be trusted as a real signal of progress.

astra-6.text:
What I learned from Kaiming is that a strong baseline is a way of thinking about a problem. Before you introduce a new idea, you need to understand how far a simple, existing approach can go when you really get it right. Otherwise, you can mistake a weak comparison for a breakthrough.

That takes patience. When something doesn’t work, it’s tempting to add another module or another loss. But each addition makes it harder to understand what’s actually happening. The more useful question is often: What is the essential difficulty here? Can we isolate it and test it with a clean experiment?

To me, that’s the connection between strong baselines and breakthroughs. A baseline doesn’t just set a higher bar; it helps you see where the real limitation is. And once you can see that clearly, the idea that moves things forward can be surprisingly simple.

r001.rationale: The response says a baseline sets a higher bar and reveals limitations, but does not state that its quality sets an upper limit on research built on it.

r002.rationale: It says a weak comparison can be mistaken for a breakthrough, clearly conveying that a weak baseline can make the apparent research signal misleading.

r003.rationale: The response recommends understanding how far a simple approach can go, but does not present improvement over the strongest achievable baseline as a test of genuine progress.

sol-6.1.text:
What I learned from Kaiming is that a strong baseline is really a way of thinking. Before you add something new, you should understand how far a simple, well-designed system can go. Have you trained it properly? Is the comparison fair? Do you actually understand where it fails?

That sounds straightforward, but it takes a lot of discipline. When your baseline is weak, almost any additional complexity can look like a contribution. When the baseline is strong, you have to confront whether your idea is doing something meaningful.

And that’s what makes breakthroughs possible. You can isolate the real bottleneck and see which change actually matters. Sometimes the important discovery is that you can remove something everyone assumed was necessary. So I don’t see building baselines as separate from creative research. It’s part of how you create the conditions for a genuinely new idea to become clear.

r001.rationale: The response says a baseline reveals how far a simple system can go, but does not state that baseline quality sets an upper limit on research built on it.

r002.rationale: It says a weak baseline can make added complexity look like a contribution, describing a misleading apparent research signal.

r003.rationale: It presents a strong baseline as the test of whether a new idea does something meaningful, which conveys using the strongest baseline to assess genuine progress.
